what_it_does: A GPU runs thousands of small programs called threads simultaneously, organized into groups called warps (32 threads that move in lockstep) and larger blocks called CTAs (Cooperative Thread Arrays). To feed all those threads quickly, the GPU has a fast on-chip memory called a cache, but threads often read overlapping data without the scheduler knowing it — so the same data gets fetched from slower main memory multiple times unnecessarily. This paper introduces VISTA, a smarter GPU scheduling algorithm that watches at runtime for cases where non-adjacent thread groups happen to need the same data, then reorders their execution so they run close together in time, turning those separate memory fetches into a single shared one. This is said to reduce wasted memory traffic for memory-intensive applications without requiring any changes to the programs themselves.
